claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Li et al., 2019; Gergelits et al., 2021).

claims.claim: ZCWPW1 is implicated in mediating efficient repair at symmetrically bound sites.
claims.source: Recent work has further implicated the gene ZCWPW1 in mediating efficient repair at symmetrically bound sites (Huang et al., 2020; Mahgoub et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Huang et al., 2020; Mahgoub et al., 2020; Wells et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The model assumes that the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9.
claims.source: Based on this premise, we model the co-evolution of PRDM9 and its binding sites from first principles, assuming, as seems realistic, that: (i) the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9, (ii) PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites (i.e. the availability of PRDM9 is limiting), and (iii) fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claims.claim: The model assumes that PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites.
claims.source: Based on this premise, we model the co-evolution of PRDM9 and its binding sites from first principles, assuming, as seems realistic, that: (i) the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9, (ii) PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites (i.e. the availability of PRDM9 is limiting), and (iii) fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claims.claim: The model assumes that fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
claims.source: Based on this premise, we model the co-evolution of PRDM9 and its binding sites from first principles, assuming, as seems realistic, that: (i) the number of DSBs is regulated independently of PRDM9, (ii) PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites (i.e. the availability of PRDM9 is limiting), and (iii) fitness is a function of the probability that the smallest chromosome experiences some minimal number of DSBs at sites symmetrically bound by PRDM9.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claims.claim: The model describes PRDM9 binding during meiosis in terms of Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
claims.source: The first describes PRDM9 binding during meiosis in terms of Michaelis-Menten kinetics, in which sites compete for binding their cognate PRDM9 proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claims.claim: In the model, sites compete for binding their cognate PRDM9 proteins.
claims.source: The first describes PRDM9 binding during meiosis in terms of Michaelis-Menten kinetics, in which sites compete for binding their cognate PRDM9 proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claims.claim: The model considers only the smallest chromosome because fitness defects arising from asymmetry in PRDM9 binding should affect the smallest chromosomes first.
claims.source: For simplicity, we consider only the smallest chromosome because fitness defects arising from asymmetry in PRDM9 binding should affect the smallest chromosomes first (assuming, as seems plausible, that they have fewer sites at which a symmetric DSB might be made).
claims.evidence: This is an explicit simplification in the model with a stated rationale.

claims.claim: Individual fitness is assumed to equal the probability of a symmetric DSB in a single meiosis.
claims.source: Also for simplicity, we assume that individual fitness is equal to the probability of a symmetric DSB in a single meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit simplification in the model.

claims.claim: Mutations that destroy the ability of a site to bind to its cognate PRDM9 are introduced with probability μ per individual meiosis.
claims.source: Lastly, we use a deterministic approximation to describe the erosion of binding sites over time (Figure 1D). Mutations that destroy the ability of a site to bind to its cognate PRDM9 are introduced with probability μ per individual meiosis and can fix in the population due to biased gene conversion.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claims.claim: The fixation probability of mutations that destroy PRDM9 binding depends on rates at which the binding site experiences a DSB and of gene conversion.
claims.source: Mutations that destroy the ability of a site to bind to its cognate PRDM9 are introduced with probability μ per individual meiosis and can fix in the population due to biased gene conversion. The fixation probability depends on rates at which the binding site experiences a DSB and of GC.
claims.evidence: This is an explicit component of the model.

claims.claim: Turnover time is inversely proportional to population size.
claims.source: Turnover time is inversely proportional to population size (Figure 6B), because the increase in mutational input at binding sites and thus the rate at which they are lost are proportional to the population size (see Equation 11); other factors, such as the mutational input at PRDM9, have negligible effects by comparison (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The turnover time is shorter for strong hotspots than for weak ones.
claims.source: The turnover time is shorter for strong hotspots than for weak ones (Figure 6B), because PRDM9 alleles with stronger hotspots enter the population with fewer hotspots (Figure 6A) and stronger hotspots experience more DSBs and are therefore lost faster.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Average PRDM9 diversity is expected to be greater in larger populations.
claims.source: Consequently, average PRDM9 diversity is expected to be greater in larger populations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model dynamics.

claims.claim: The cycling dynamics characteristic of PRDM9 evolution entails a substantial genetic load.
claims.source: The cycling dynamics characteristic of PRDM9 evolution over much of the parameter space entails a substantial genetic load, i.e., an average fitness that is substantially lower than its optimal value (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Average fitness is greater in smaller populations than in larger ones.
claims.source: Moreover, in contrast to the usual case, in this setting, average fitness is greater in smaller populations than in larger ones, as the number of hotspots – and thus the fitness associated with the predominant PRDM9 alleles when they fix and when they exit the population – is lower in larger populations than in smaller ones (Figures 5 and 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figures 5 and 6A.

claims.claim: Previous models assumed that the loss of PRDM9 binding sites leads to a reduction in the number of DSBs.
claims.source: Previous models of PRDM9 evolution demonstrated how selection to maintain a given rate of recombination (e.g., for there to be at least one crossover per chromosome) can act as a countervailing force to the loss of hotspots through gene conversion, and ensure the persistence of hotspots (Ubeda and Wilkins, 2011; Latrille et al., 2017). These models were based on an assumption now believed to be incorrect, however: that the loss of PRDM9 binding sites leads to a reduction in the number of DSBs.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous models with citations (Ubeda and Wilkins, 2011; Latrille et al., 2017).

claims.claim: When hotspots are lost, PRDM9 simply binds elsewhere.
claims.source: Since DSB formation is regulated independently of PRDM9 (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019) and hotspots are thought to compete for binding (Diagouraga et al., 2018), it more plausible that when hotspots are lost, PRDM9 simply binds elsewhere.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence (Kauppi et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2017; Brick et al., 2012; Mihola et al., 2019; Diagouraga et al., 2018).

claims.claim: In the model, the selection driving the evolution of the PRDM9 ZF arises from the requirement of symmetric binding in DSB repair.
claims.source: In our model, the selection driving the evolution of the PRDM9 ZF arises from the requirement of symmetric binding in DSB repair, and thus from changes in the shape of its binding distribution over time, rather than from changes in net binding, as previously assumed.
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion from the model.

claims.claim: Strong hotspots are lost more rapidly than weak ones.
claims.source: Strong hotspots are lost more rapidly than weak ones, resulting in a shift from a small number of strong binding sites to a larger number of weak binding sites over the lifespan of a PRDM9 allele.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claims.claim: The shift from strong to weak binding sites entails a reduction in the number of symmetric DSBs.
claims.source: Strong hotspots are lost more rapidly than weak ones, resulting in a shift from a small number of strong binding sites to a larger number of weak binding sites over the lifespan of a PRDM9 allele. This shift entails a reduction in the number of symmetric DSBs, and eventually selection in favor of a new PRDM9 allele.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claims.claim: New PRDM9 alleles are favored because they redirect PRDM9 binding to a smaller proportion of the genome, making symmetric binding more likely.
claims.source: They are favored because, in doing so, PRDM9 binding is redirected to a smaller proportion of the genome, and is therefore more likely to bind symmetrically.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the model.

claims.claim: The sites most likely to be symmetrically bound will also experience the highest rates of drive.
claims.source: Accordingly, the sites most likely to be symmetrically bound will also experience the highest rates of drive, in accordance with empirical observations (Hinch et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the model supported by citation (Hinch et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The loss of hotspots results in PRDM9 binding becoming more dispersed across the genome.
claims.source: In our two-heat model, when hotspots are lost, PRDM9 binding shifts towards the more plentiful class of weak binding sites. Given a more realistic distribution of heats, we would similarly expect the loss of hotspots to result in PRDM9 binding becoming more dispersed across the genome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model extended to more realistic scenarios.

claims.claim: The number of hotspots will increase over time as optimal binding motifs erode.
claims.source: After the optimal binding motifs have eroded, most PRDM9 binding will plausibly shifts toward the next best and larger class of motifs, with one mismatch, and then those with two mismatches, and so on. This consideration suggests that the number of hotspots will increase over time (although the extent to which binding becomes more dispersed will depend on the degree to which PRDM9 binding is limiting).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model extended to more realistic scenarios.

claims.claim: The heat of observed hotspots should decrease over time.
claims.source: This picture is in stark contrast with the previous understanding of the evolution of hotspots, namely, that gene conversion leads to a reduction in the number of hotspots over time. It further suggests that the heat of observed hotspots should decrease over time.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model.

claims.claim: In all species with a complete PRDM9 investigated to date, PRDM9 diversity appears to be high relative to other ZF genes, regardless of the effective population size.
claims.source: In all species with a complete PRDM9 investigated to date, PRDM9 diversity appears to be high relative to other ZF genes, regardless of the effective population size (Buard et al., 2014; Vara et al., 2019; Alleva et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Buard et al., 2014; Vara et al., 2019; Alleva et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The rate of mutation at the PRDM9 ZF array has been inferred to be quite high, with a ZF copy number change of ~0.3–20 x 10–5 per generation.
claims.source: The rate of mutation at the PRDM9 ZF array has been inferred to be quite high, with a ZF copy number change of ~0.3–20 x 10–5 per generation (Jeffreys et al., 2013), as expected from its minisatellite nature.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation (Jeffreys et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Strong signatures of erosion at binding sites associated with PRDM9 alleles in several species seem indicative of a cycling dynamic.
claims.source: The strong signatures of erosion at binding sites associated with PRDM9 alleles in several species (Myers et al., 2010; Smagulova et al., 2016; Hoge et al., 2023) seem indicative of a cycling dynamic.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence (Myers et al., 2010; Smagulova et al., 2016; Hoge et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Being heterozygote for a minor PRDM9 ZFs is protective against azoospermia in humans.
claims.source: In turn, anecdotal evidence suggests that being heterozygote for a minor PRDM9 ZFs is protective against azoospermia in humans (Irie et al., 2009), and the high levels of PRDM9 diversity seen across species with very different effective population sizes might suggest that the dynamics are closer to expectations for strong hotspots.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation (Irie et al., 2009).

claims.source: Most empirical manipulations that rescue fertility in otherwise sterile crosses of hybrid mice can be readily understood as restoring symmetric binding (Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Davies et al., 2016; Gregorova et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Fertility can be restored by increasing the expression of either PRDM9 allele present in sterile hybrids.

claims.claim: Fertility can be restored by removing one PRDM9 allele but not the other in sterile hybrids.

claims.evidence: Supported by citation (Flachs et al., 2012).

claims.claim: In sterile hybrids, available PRDM9 is being sequestered to the non-parental genetic background, where their strongest binding sites have not been eroded.
claims.source: In the sterile hybrids, no sites experience a symmetric DSB on the smallest chromosome. Nonetheless, binding sites for both alleles occur on their respective parental backgrounds, as evidenced by their use in the parental mice. Why then are they not used in the hybrids? We suggest that the reason is because PRDM9 is limiting, and the available PRDM9 is being sequestered to the non-parental genetic background, where their strongest binding sites have not been eroded.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: Increasing PRDM9 expression of either allele results in more PRDM9 binding at parental binding sites, allowing for symmetric binding.
claims.source: Increasing PRDM9 expression of either allele results in more PRDM9 binding at parental binding sites, allowing for symmetric binding.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation proposed by the authors based on the model.

claims.claim: The evolutionary benefit of PRDM9 binding symmetrically plausibly stems from the preferentially use of the same loci on one chromosome for DSB initiation and, on the homologous chromosome, for DSB repair.
claims.source: Given recent findings, the evolutionary benefit of PRDM9 binding symmetrically plausibly stems from the preferentially use of the same loci on one chromosome for DSB initiation and, on the homologous chromosome, for DSB repair (see Introduction).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on recent findings discussed in the Introduction.

claims.claim: This strategy improves the efficacy of both homolog pairing and DSB repair, potentially by reducing the search space during homolog engagement and/or by increasing the accessibility of the loci for strand invasion and subsequent steps of repair.
claims.source: This strategy improves the efficacy of both homolog pairing and DSB repair, potentially by reducing the search space during homolog engagement and/or by increasing the accessibility of the loci for strand invasion and subsequent steps of repair.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claims.claim: The advantage of hotspots may be to limit recombination to a small proportion of the genome.

claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from Davies et al., 2016 with supporting citation (Singhal et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Taxa with DSB-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing, such as Drosophila or C. elegans, do not have hotspots.
claims.source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that taxa with DSB-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing, such as Drosophila or C. elegans, do not have hotspots (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015; Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016), whereas most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms, such as most yeast, plants or vertebrates, do (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015; Tock and Henderson, 2018; Liu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015; Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016).

claims.claim: Most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms of homolog pairing have hotspots.
claims.source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that taxa with DSB-independent mechanisms of homolog pairing, such as Drosophila or C. elegans, do not have hotspots (Manzano-Winkler et al., 2013; Smukowski Heil et al., 2015; Kaur and Rockman, 2014; Bernstein and Rockman, 2016), whereas most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms, such as most yeast, plants or vertebrates, do (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015; Tock and Henderson, 2018; Liu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Yelina et al., 2015; Tock and Henderson, 2018; Liu et al., 2019).

claims.claim: PRDM9 arose prior to the common ancestor of animals and has since been repeatedly lost, including more than a dozen times across vertebrates.
claims.source: PRDM9 arose prior to the common ancestor of animals and has since been repeatedly lost, including more than a dozen times across vertebrates (Baker et al., 2017; Cavassim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Baker et al., 2017; Cavassim et al., 2022).

claims.claim: In vertebrate lineages in which PRDM9 has been lost, recombination events are concentrated in hotspots that tend to be found associated with promoter-like features of the genome.
claims.source: In vertebrate lineages in which PRDM9 has been lost, such as canids, birds or percomorph fish, as well as in PRDM9 knockout mice and rats, and to a minor degree in sterile mice hybrids, recombination events are concentrated in hotspots that tend to be found associated with promoter-like features of the genome, such as transcriptional start sites and/or CpG-islands (Brick et al., 2012; Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Mihola et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations (Brick et al., 2012; Auton et al., 2013; Singhal et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016; Mihola et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The mechanism for localizing hotspots to promoter-like features is likely ancestral to the evolution of PRDM9's role in recombination.
claims.source: Therefore, this mechanism for localizing hotspots is likely ancestral to the evolution of PRDM9's role in recombination, and is retained in the presence of PRDM9.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that this mechanism is found in lineages without PRDM9.

claims.claim: The two mechanisms for localizing hotspots may be engaged in a tug of war, the outcome of which is more lopsided in mice and humans and more even in other species, such as snakes.
claims.source: Indeed, recent work suggests that the two mechanisms may be engaged in a tug of war, the outcome of which is more lopsided in mice and humans and more even in other species, such as snakes (Hoge et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation (Hoge et al., 2023).

claims.claim: PRDM9 may be favored when it further enhances the degree of symmetric recruitment of factors involved in both DSB initiation and DSB repair relative to that of default hotspots.
claims.source: If species without PRDM9 also recruit factors involved in both DSB initiation and DSB repair on both homologs, then PRDM9 may be favored when it further enhances the degree of symmetric recruitment of such factors relative to that of default hotspots, that is when PRDM9-mediated hotspots are fewer and hotter than default hotspots given the same number of DSBs.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation.

claims.claim: DSB heats measured by DMC1 ChIP-seq are higher in wild type than in PRDM9-/- mice.
claims.source: In support of this possibility, DSB heats measured by DMC1 ChIP-seq are higher in wild type than in PRDM9-/- mice (Brick et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation (Brick et al., 2012).

claims.claim: PRDM9 may enable the successful completion of meiosis with fewer DSBs.
claims.source: If PRDM9 improves the efficiency of DSB-dependent homolog engagement, it may also enable the successful completion of meiosis with fewer DSBs—a potentially important secondary benefit, given that DSBs pose an inherent danger to cellular survival (Cooper et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation with supporting citation (Cooper et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Not all strains of mice are sterile when PRDM9 is knocked out, and those which are tend to have fewer DSBs per meiosis.
claims.source: Notably, not all strains of mice are sterile when PRDM9 is knocked out, and those which are tend to have fewer DSBs per meiosis (Mihola et al., 2019), which seems to support the hypothesis that PRDM9 may be especially important for the successful completion of meiosis with fewer DSBs.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation (Mihola et al., 2019).

results.result: PRDM9 determines DSB hotspot locations through its zinc finger array DNA-binding specificity, which is rapidly evolving. PRDM9 binds thousands of sites during meiosis, catalyzes histone modifications, and facilitates DSB formation by SPO11 at a subset of bound sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C13-C16 describe well-established background knowledge about PRDM9 function, supported by extensive citations to prior experimental work. These claims provide the biological foundation for the model but are not novel findings of this manuscript.

results.result: Species lacking PRDM9 show conserved recombination landscapes near promoter-like features over millions of years, while PRDM9-using species show rapidly evolving recombination landscapes with no overlap between closely related species.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 summarize well-documented differences in recombination patterns between species with and without PRDM9, supported by multiple citations. This is established background knowledge rather than a novel finding.

results.result: Gene conversion causes under-transmission of hot alleles at PRDM9 binding sites, leading to rapid erosion of these sites. Different PRDM9 alleles are associated with different hotspot usage patterns, and positive selection drives rapid PRDM9 evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 describe the evolutionary dynamics of PRDM9 and its binding sites based on extensive prior work. All claims are well-supported by citations and represent established knowledge motivating the current study.

results.result: DSB formation is regulated independently of PRDM9, with similar numbers of DSBs in PRDM9-/- individuals. PRDM9 binding sites compete for available PRDM9 molecules, and loss of binding sites causes PRDM9 to bind elsewhere rather than reducing total DSB numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 establish key biological constraints that distinguish this model from previous ones. All claims are supported by citations to experimental work, providing the empirical foundation for the model's assumptions.

results.result: PRDM9 plays a role in DSB repair through symmetric recruitment to homologous chromosomes. Asymmetric binding in sterile hybrids causes meiotic defects, while restoring symmetry rescues fertility. DSBs at asymmetrically-bound sites experience delayed repair and reduced crossover formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C42 summarize recent experimental findings on PRDM9's role in symmetric binding and DSB repair, all supported by extensive citations. This background motivates the model's focus on symmetric binding as a fitness determinant.

results.result: The model assumes DSB numbers are regulated independently of PRDM9, PRDM9 binding is competitive between sites, and fitness depends on symmetric DSBs on the smallest chromosome. PRDM9 binding follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics with competitive binding, and mutations at binding sites fix through gene conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C53 describe the model's core assumptions and mathematical framework. These are clearly stated and justified based on empirical observations (C28-C42). The assumptions are reasonable given current biological knowledge, though some simplifications are acknowledged.

results.result: Loss of strong binding sites leads to use of more numerous weaker sites, causing a sharp reduction in symmetric binding. This favors new PRDM9 alleles that restore a smaller set of strong binding sites. The advantage is in limiting binding site numbers rather than increasing total PRDM9 binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 present the model's central mechanistic insight. The logic is sound given the model's assumptions about competitive binding and symmetric DSB requirements. Figures 2-3 demonstrate this mechanism, showing how fitness depends non-monotonically on hotspot numbers.

results.result: Selection for PRDM9 evolution arises from the requirement for symmetric binding in DSB repair, not from changes in net binding. Strong hotspots are lost faster than weak ones, causing a shift to weaker sites that reduces symmetric DSBs. New alleles are favored because they redirect binding to a smaller genomic proportion, increasing symmetric binding probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 articulate the model's key theoretical contribution, distinguishing it from previous models. The logic follows from the competitive binding framework and is supported by simulation results in Figures 4-6. Claim C72 is additionally supported by empirical citation.

results.result: PRDM9 turnover time is inversely proportional to population size and shorter for strong hotspots. Average PRDM9 diversity is greater in larger populations. The cycling dynamics entail substantial genetic load, with paradoxically higher average fitness in smaller populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 describe quantitative predictions from the model, supported by simulation results in Figures 5-6. The inverse relationship with population size follows logically from the model structure (Equation 11). The counterintuitive fitness pattern is well-explained by the dynamics.

results.result: Previous models incorrectly assumed that loss of PRDM9 binding sites reduces DSB numbers. The current model recognizes that when hotspots are lost, PRDM9 simply binds elsewhere, based on evidence that DSB formation is regulated independently of PRDM9.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 correctly characterize the key difference from previous models (Ubeda and Wilkins 2011; Latrille et al. 2017) and justify the new approach based on empirical evidence (C28-C32). This distinction is fundamental to the model's novelty.

results.result: Loss of hotspots results in more dispersed PRDM9 binding across the genome. The number of hotspots will increase over time as optimal motifs erode and binding shifts to motifs with mismatches. The heat of observed hotspots should decrease over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 extend the two-heat model to more realistic continuous distributions of binding affinities. While the logic is plausible, these predictions are speculative extrapolations beyond what the two-heat model directly demonstrates. The authors acknowledge this uncertainty in the Discussion.

results.result: PRDM9 diversity is high across species regardless of population size. The mutation rate at PRDM9 is high due to its minisatellite nature. Erosion signatures at binding sites suggest cycling dynamics. Heterozygosity for minor PRDM9 alleles may protect against azoospermia in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 summarize empirical observations relevant to evaluating the model's predictions. All are supported by citations. These observations are consistent with the model but do not definitively validate it, as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: Most fertility rescue manipulations in sterile hybrid mice restore symmetric binding. The model explains why increasing PRDM9 expression or removing specific alleles can rescue fertility: PRDM9 is sequestered to non-parental backgrounds where strong sites remain, and increasing expression allows binding at parental sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 apply the model to explain empirical observations about hybrid sterility. The explanation is logically consistent with the model's competitive binding framework. However, C83-C84 are speculative interpretations rather than tested predictions.

results.result: The evolutionary advantage of hotspots may be to increase DSB repair and homolog pairing efficiency by limiting recombination to a small genomic proportion. Symmetric PRDM9 binding improves efficacy by reducing search space during homolog engagement and increasing locus accessibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C85-C87 present speculative hypotheses about the ultimate evolutionary advantage of hotspots. While consistent with the model and some empirical observations, these are not directly tested. The authors appropriately present these as speculative extensions.

results.result: Taxa with DSB-independent homolog pairing mechanisms lack hotspots, while most species with DSB-dependent mechanisms have hotspots. PRDM9 arose before the animal ancestor and has been repeatedly lost. In PRDM9-loss lineages, recombination localizes to promoter-like features via an ancestral mechanism that may compete with PRDM9.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 summarize comparative evolutionary patterns across taxa, all supported by citations. These observations provide broader context for understanding PRDM9 evolution and are consistent with the model's framework.

results.result: PRDM9 may be favored when it enhances symmetric recruitment beyond default hotspots, creating fewer but hotter hotspots. PRDM9 may enable successful meiosis with fewer DSBs, which is supported by observations that sterile PRDM9-/- mouse strains tend to have fewer DSBs.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 present speculative hypotheses about why PRDM9 is maintained or lost in different lineages. While C95 and C97 cite supporting evidence, the overall explanation remains speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge these as open questions.

results.result: Recombination is more uniformly distributed across the genome in Drosophila and C. elegans compared to species with hotspots.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 state well-established facts about recombination patterns in these model organisms, supported by citations. This provides context for why hotspot evolution is an interesting question.
